questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following glucose transporter in the myocytes is under the influence of insulin?
questions.explanation: GLUT 4 is the glucose transporter in the myocytes under the influence of insulin. Glucose transport in the body mainly occurs through sodium-independent glucose transporters, which include GLUT transporters and, to a small extent, sodium-dependent glucose transporters present in the small intestine. Insulin induces movement of intracellular GLUT 4 molecules to the cell surface and thus increases glucose uptake. In type 2 diabetes mellitus, membrane GLUT 4 is reduced, leading to insulin resistance in muscle and fat cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In a patient after overnight fasting, which of the following will have reduced levels of glucose transporters?
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue will have reduced levels of glucose transporters after overnight fasting. Passive uptake of glucose by myocytes and adipose tissue is catalyzed by the GLUT-4 transporter. Levels of insulin-sensitive receptor GLUT-4 decrease after overnight fasting. In the absence of insulin, most GLUT 4 molecules are sequestered in membrane vesicles within the cell; when blood glucose rises, release of insulin triggers GLUT 4 movement to the plasma membrane.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is false about glycolysis?

options.text: 2 ATPs are utilized in the pathway

questions.explanation: The complete breakdown of glucose involves the Krebs cycle (TCA cycle), which occurs in mitochondria, and not glycolysis. Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm of all cells. A 6-carbon glucose is converted into 3-carbon pyruvate in a ten-step anaerobic pathway. RBCs lack mitochondria and completely rely on glucose for energy. Phosphofructokinase-1 is the rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis and is involved in conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. The irreversible steps are catalyzed by hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase. Two ATP are utilized in glycolysis. Net ATP from aerobic glycolysis is 7 ATP. Inhibitors noted in the source include iodoacetate for glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, fluoride for enolase, and arsenite at the 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate kinase step, causing glycolysis to produce zero net ATP.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following substances inhibits the rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis?
questions.explanation: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is the rate-limiting enzyme in glycolysis. Citrate inhibits PFK-1. Mg2+ serves as a co-factor. In general, end products can inhibit forward reactions by product inhibition. Inhibitors of PFK-1 include ATP and citrate. Allosteric activators include ADP, AMP, and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (the most potent activator). Hormonal regulation: insulin induces and glucagon represses.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: All of the following statements about glucokinase are true in comparison to other hexokinases, except:
questions.explanation: Glucose is the only cellular substrate that can be phosphorylated by glucokinase. Glucokinase has a higher Vmax and higher Km value than hexokinase, requiring a higher concentration of glucose for half saturation. Hence glucokinase functions only when intracellular glucose concentration is high, as immediately after a carbohydrate-rich meal. Compared with hexokinase: glucokinase is in liver and pancreatic beta cells, has high Km and high Vmax, is not inhibited by G6P, and is inducible. Hexokinase is in most tissues, has low Km and low Vmax, is inhibited by G6P, and is not inducible. The source notes that glucokinase can act on other hexoses such as fructose and mannose, but because its Km for these reactions is high, this is not significant; therefore the best option has been chosen as given in the source answer key.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is the first committed step of glycolysis?
questions.explanation: Fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate catalyzed by PFK-1 is the first committed step of glycolysis. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate once formed cannot revert back and enter another pathway. Glucose to glucose-6-phosphate is also irreversible, catalyzed by hexokinase, but glucose-6-phosphate can still enter the HMP shunt and is therefore not a committed step of glycolysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding anaerobic glycolysis?

options.text: Occurs in places like the eye lens and RBCs

questions.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase, not pyruvate dehydrogenase, is needed in anaerobic glycolysis. Under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate is reduced to lactate; this regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. RBCs lack mitochondria and therefore the further reactions of pyruvate in the TCA cycle cannot take place. Net ATP produced per glucose under anaerobic conditions is 2. Anaerobic glycolysis is the major source of ATP in RBCs and occurs in poorly vascularized structures such as lens, cornea, leukocytes, renal medulla, testes, and exercising muscle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following enzymes takes part in substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis?
questions.explanation: The enzyme involved in substrate-level phosphorylation at this step is pyruvate kinase. In substrate-level phosphorylation, direct generation of ATP occurs. questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: How many net ATPs are generated in aerobic glycolysis?
questions.explanation: Net generation of ATP up to pyruvate in aerobic glycolysis is 7 ATP. Two ATP are utilized in the earlier steps catalyzed by hexokinase and PFK-1. ATP-producing steps include glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (5 ATP equivalent from 2 NADH), 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate (2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation), and phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate (2 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation), giving 9 ATP produced and 7 ATP net.

questions.question: You are collecting a blood sample from a patient for blood glucose estimation. You put the sample in a vacutainer containing sodium fluoride. Which of the following enzyme is inhibited by this compound?

The source also lists iodoacetate as an inhibitor of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and arsenite as an inhibitor of phosphoglycerate kinase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: What is fructose-2,6-bisphosphate?
questions.explanation: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent positive allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 and an inhibitor of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase. It is not an intermediate of glycolysis. It is formed by phosphorylation of fructose-6-phosphate by phosphofructokinase-2 and acts as an intracellular signal indicating abundant glucose, thereby increasing glycolysis during the fed state.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient with anemia and hepatosplenomegaly is diagnosed with hemolytic anemia. Deficiency of which of the following glycolytic enzymes is most likely associated with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Deficiency of pyruvate kinase leads to hemolytic anemia. Erythrocytes lack mitochondria and generate ATP exclusively by glycolysis. A deficiency of a glycolytic enzyme reduces the ATP available to RBC membranes, decreasing deformability and causing removal by the reticuloendothelial system, leading to hemolytic anemia. The source notes pyruvate kinase as the second most common enzyme deficiency causing hemolytic anemia after glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Where does the Rapoport-Luebering cycle occur?
questions.explanation: The Rapoport-Luebering cycle (2,3-BPG shunt) occurs in RBCs. 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate is converted to 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate by bisphosphoglycerate mutase. 2,3-BPG is present at high concentration in RBCs and decreases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen, promoting oxygen release in hypoxia. 2,3-BPG is hydrolyzed to 3-phosphoglycerate. Because the phosphoglycerate kinase step is bypassed, no ATP is generated in that step; anaerobic glycolysis through this shunt yields no net ATP.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following pathways acts as a major energy source for cancer cells?
questions.explanation: Cancer cells derive energy mainly from glycolysis. Cancer cells utilize large amounts of glucose and metabolize it to lactic acid even in the presence of oxygen (Warburg effect). The increased rate of glycolysis results from impaired mitochondrial electron transport and supports proliferation in reduced-oxygen conditions. Increased glucose consumption is also used as a carbon source for anabolic processes. This effect is the basis for detecting cancers by FDG-PET scanning.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In which of the following tissues does gluconeogenesis take place?
questions.explanation: The liver and kidney are the two major locations where gluconeogenesis takes place. During short periods of fasting, most gluconeogenesis occurs in the liver; with longer fasting the kidney becomes a major site. Gluconeogenesis synthesizes glucose or glycogen from non-carbohydrate precursors such as glucogenic amino acids, lactate, glycerol, and propionate. Lactate from tissues is transported to liver and reconverted to glucose in the Cori cycle. Muscle cannot participate in gluconeogenesis because it lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is not a substrate for gluconeogenesis?
questions.explanation: Acetyl CoA is not a substrate for gluconeogenesis; instead it enters the Krebs cycle for oxidative phosphorylation. Substrates for gluconeogenesis include glucogenic amino acids (alanine is the major contributor), glucogenic amino acids that enter via pyruvate, oxaloacetate, succinyl CoA, and alpha-ketoglutarate, lactate, pyruvate, glycerol, and propionate in ruminants.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: What is the process of reconversion of lactate formed in the muscles and RBCs, back into glucose inside the liver called?
questions.explanation: The process of reconversion of lactate formed in muscle and RBCs back into glucose inside the liver is the Cori cycle. Lactic acid is formed from pyruvate during anaerobic glycolysis and transported to the liver, where it is reconverted to glucose; this entire process is called the Cori cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following organ pairs is involved in the Cahill cycle?
questions.explanation: The liver and muscle are involved in the Cahill cycle. During fasting, alanine is produced in skeletal muscle by transamination reactions from pyruvate, released into circulation, enters the liver, and is reconverted to pyruvate. This pyruvate serves as a substrate for gluconeogenesis. The pathway is also called the glucose-alanine cycle.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Malate shuttle is important in which of the following processes?
questions.explanation: The malate shuttle is important in both gluconeogenesis and glycolysis. It transfers reducing equivalents across the impermeable inner mitochondrial membrane. In glycolysis, NADH produced in the cytosol is transferred into mitochondria via malate. In gluconeogenesis, pyruvate in mitochondria generates oxaloacetate, which is converted to aspartate and translocated to the cytosol via the malate shuttle for synthesis of glucose.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is a repressor of the enzyme pyruvate carboxylase?
questions.explanation: Insulin is a repressor of the enzyme pyruvate carboxylase. Pyruvate carboxylase is a gluconeogenic enzyme whose activity increases during fasting and decreases after carbohydrate feeding. The source table lists glucocorticoids, glucagon, and epinephrine as inducers; insulin as repressor; acetyl CoA as activator; and ADP as inhibitor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: All of the following enzymes are involved in gluconeogenesis except:
questions.explanation: Phosphoglucomutase is not involved in gluconeogenesis. It catalyzes conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate, which is important for glycogenesis, glycogenolysis, and the uronic acid pathway. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, pyruvate carboxylase, and phosphoglycerate kinase participate in gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is a step in the gluconeogenic pathway?
questions.explanation: Oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate is an important irreversible step in gluconeogenesis. GTP is utilized and CO2 is liberated. The reaction occurs in the cytoplasm and is catalyzed by PEP carboxykinase. Pyruvate to lactate is an anaerobic glycolytic reaction; glucose-6-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate is a glycolytic step; pyruvate to acetyl CoA is an anaerobic step in oxidation of glucose as stated in the source.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is not seen in low insulin:glucagon ratio?
questions.explanation: A low insulin:glucagon ratio indicates low insulin and high glucagon, as in fasting. In fasting, glycogen breakdown, ketogenesis, and gluconeogenesis increase, while glycogen storage decreases. The source table contrasts fasting/low insulin:glucagon ratio with fed/high insulin:glucagon ratio: gluconeogenesis increased vs decreased, and glycogen storage decreased vs increased.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following enzyme activity decreases in fasting?
questions.explanation: During fasting, because insulin is low, phosphofructokinase-1 activity is inhibited. PFK-1 is a glycolytic enzyme induced by insulin in the well-fed state. Hormone-sensitive lipase mobilizes stored fats and is active in fasting. Glycogen phosphorylase is active in fasting to produce glucose from glycogen. Pyruvate carboxylase is a gluconeogenic enzyme activated during fasting; its activity rises as hepatic acetyl CoA increases from fatty acid oxidation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Enzyme activated by a decrease in insulin:glucagon ratio is:
questions.explanation: The enzyme activated by a decrease in the insulin:glucagon ratio is glucose-6-phosphatase. A decrease in this ratio is seen in fasting, when gluconeogenesis and inhibition of glycolysis occur. Glucose-6-phosphatase is a gluconeogenic enzyme and is activated; glucokinase, hexokinase, and phosphofructokinase are glycolytic enzymes and are inhibited in the fasting state.
